subject: community-medicine
title: Sampling Methods: Simple Random, Systematic, Stratified, Cluster, and Sample Size

steps.title: Why sampling, and the sampling frame
steps.tx: Studying everyone is usually impossible, so researchers study a sample drawn from a complete list of the population called the **sampling frame** (electoral rolls, village registers, admission lists). Every sampling error story begins here: an incomplete or outdated frame (telephone directories missing the poor) biases results before fieldwork starts, however elegant the statistics that follow.
steps.say: The sampling frame is the list you draw from. A faulty list dooms the study before it begins.

nodes.label: Build or verify the sampling frame

steps.title: Simple random sampling
steps.tx: **Simple random sampling** gives every population member an equal, independent chance of selection, classically by lottery or random number tables and today by computer generators. It needs a complete numbered frame, suits small homogeneous populations, and underpins the theory of all fancier designs. Its weakness is logistical: selected households may scatter across a district, raising travel cost per interview.
steps.say: Simple random sampling is a fair lottery from a full list. Equal chance for all, but scattered selections cost travel.

steps.title: Systematic random sampling
steps.tx: **Systematic random sampling** picks a random start between one and k, then every kth name from the list, where k equals population divided by desired sample (the sampling interval). It spreads the sample evenly through the frame and needs no random number for each pick. The trap is periodicity: if the list itself cycles with period k (every tenth house a corner shop), the sample distorts badly.
steps.say: Take a random start, then every kth name. Beware lists with hidden cycles matching your interval.

nodes.label: Compute interval k equals N over n

steps.title: Stratified random sampling
steps.tx: Dividing the population into homogeneous strata (age groups, sex, urban rural, disease severity) and sampling randomly within each gives **stratified random sampling**. It guarantees representation of small but important groups, permits stratum specific estimates, and usually improves precision when strata differ strongly. Proportional allocation mirrors population shares; disproportionate allocation oversamples rare strata and reweights in analysis.
steps.say: Stratify first, sample inside each stratum. Small important groups can no longer be missed by chance.

rows: Precise rare group estimate, reweight later

steps.title: Cluster sampling and the 30 by 7 design
steps.tx: **Cluster sampling** selects groups (villages, wards, schools) randomly, then studies members within chosen clusters, trading statistical efficiency for feasibility. The World Health Organization's classic thirty cluster by seven children design assessed immunisation coverage for decades: thirty clusters, seven children each, two hundred ten total. Clustering inflates variance through the design effect because neighbours resemble one another.
steps.say: Sample villages, not scattered children, and fieldwork becomes possible. Thirty clusters of seven built the classic coverage survey.

steps.title: Multistage sampling in national surveys
steps.tx: India's National Family Health Survey chains stages in **multistage sampling**: districts or villages first (often probability proportional to size), then households, then eligible individuals. Each stage uses the practical frame available at that level. Multistage designs are the only feasible route to nationally representative data in a billion plus population, at the price of complex weights and clustered variance.
steps.say: National surveys sample in stages: areas, then households, then people. Weights repair the unequal chances afterwards.

nodes.label: Stage 1: villages or wards by size

steps.title: Non probability sampling and its place
steps.tx: **Non probability sampling** (convenience samples of clinic attenders, purposive selection of typical villages, quota filling, and snowball chains through social networks for hidden populations such as injecting drug users) cannot support population estimates or standard errors. It still serves pilot work, qualitative research, and rare hidden groups where no frame exists, provided conclusions stay modest and honestly labelled.
steps.say: Convenience and snowball samples cannot estimate population rates. Use them for pilots and hidden groups, label them honestly.

steps.title: Sampling and non sampling errors
steps.tx: The gap between sample estimate and truth splits into **sampling error** (chance variation shrinking with root n, measured by the standard error) and non sampling error (bad frames, non response, lying, faulty instruments, observer bias), which grows with sloppy scale. Doubling a careless survey doubles its non sampling error while barely denting bias, the deepest lesson in survey design.
steps.say: Chance error shrinks with size; bias does not. A bigger careless survey is precisely wrong.

left.title: Sampling error
points: Pure chance of who was picked

steps.title: Sample size calculation essentials
steps.tx: The standard **sample size calculation for a prevalence survey** needs expected prevalence, allowable error (precision), and confidence level: n equals z squared times p times q divided by d squared, inflated for design effect and non response. For comparing means or proportions, expected difference and power enter instead. Underpowered studies waste every rupee; the formula is the ethics committee's first question for good reason.
steps.say: Prevalence, precision, and confidence fix the sample size. Add room for clustering and refusals before you finalise.
